threads.thread_goal: Align on current routines and main pain points before designing the new schedule.

messages.text: Morning all, kicking off this channel for the integrated daily routine for paediatric ward and childcare unit (project_pack_ref: Integrated Daily Routine for Paediatric Ward and Childcare Unit). For T1 we need to map how our days actually run now in both areas so A1 can be accurate. Can you share your current rough timeline (wake up, meds support, hygiene, play, meals, rest, evening wind-down) and where things feel messy or unsafe? I will start a draft for A1 later today and plug in what you share.

Here is the paeds ward day from my side on early shift: 07:00–08:00 handover, quick safety checks, some kids already awake and need toileting and wash. 08:00–09:00 breakfast trays, meds round overlaps so we try not to move kids too much. 09:00–11:00 washing, bed changes, some play in rooms or corridor. 11:30–12:30 lunch, again overlapping with procedures. 13:00–15:00 rest/quiet time but often interrupted by tests. 15:00–17:00 more play, visitors, snacks. 17:30–18:30 dinner. 19:00–20:00 evening wash, settle. Pain points: hygiene tasks get squeezed when procedures run late, and snack times are inconsistent so some kids are hungry during bloods or physio. Also communication with childcare unit about when kids come over is not always clear.

From the childcare unit side: 08:00–09:00 arrivals from ward and families, free play while we settle everyone. 09:30–10:00 snack. 10:00–11:30 planned activity (craft, group game) but this often gets cut when children are called back for appointments. 11:30–12:00 tidy and handwashing. 12:00–12:30 lunch. 12:30–14:00 rest/quiet play. 14:00–15:30 outdoor or movement activity if possible. 15:30–16:00 snack and pick-ups. Pain points: we do not always know when the ward needs children back, so we repeat explanations and some kids get upset when they are pulled out mid-activity. Also cleaning toys after mixed groups is hard to keep consistent on busy days.

On late shifts in the ward I see: 13:00–14:00 handover and quick room checks, 14:00–16:00 play and some therapies, 16:00–17:00 snack and visitors, 17:30–18:30 dinner, 18:30–20:00 baths or washes and settling. One issue is we are not always sure who is responsible for cleaning shared play corners and wheelchairs between uses. Sometimes it is done twice, sometimes not at all. Another pain point is handover notes: mood and appetite are not always written down, so the next shift may miss that a child refused meals twice.

For me mornings are mostly: helping with breakfast, then washing kids and changing beds, then some playtime if there is space. I am not sure about the exact times for all meds and tests, it changes a lot. A pain point I notice is when we are still washing and meals arrive, so trays wait in the corridor. Also sometimes I forget to note when toys were last cleaned, so it is hard to track.

Thanks all, this is really helpful. I will start structuring A1 around morning, midday, afternoon, evening blocks for both ward and childcare so T1 can be ticked off. Before that, can we list the tasks that absolutely must appear in the integrated routine, regardless of timing? Off the top of my head: personal hygiene (wash, teeth, toileting), bed/linen changes, meals and snacks, medication and procedures, play/activities, rest/quiet time, cleaning of rooms and toys, handovers between shifts and between ward and childcare. Anything missing from that core list?

I would add vital signs and basic observations where we support nurses, plus emotional support moments like story time or one-to-one reassurance for anxious kids. Also we should include hygiene for shared equipment: hoists, wheelchairs, play mats. For me these are core, not nice-to-have, because they link directly to safety and comfort.

From the childcare side I would explicitly call out: arrivals and departures with families, emotional check-in when children arrive from the ward, and transitions back to the ward. Also toileting and handwashing around activities and meals. These are part of what keeps children settled and reduce incidents.

Agree with what is listed. Maybe we should also include time for documenting in notes and using the future handover template, so it does not get squeezed out. Even if it is just a short slot near shift end.
I think we covered most things. Maybe also include time to explain the routine to new kids and parents, because that can take a while and we often just squeeze it in.

Let me summarise the core daily tasks we have so far so we can lock them in for the integrated routine: 1) personal hygiene (wash, teeth, toileting, evening wash), 2) bed and linen changes, 3) meals and snacks, 4) medication and procedures (timed with nursing team), 5) vital signs and basic observations support, 6) play and structured activities, 7) rest and quiet time, 8) cleaning and disinfection of rooms, toys, and shared equipment, 9) arrivals and departures with families, 10) emotional check-ins and comfort time, 11) transitions between ward and childcare, 12) documentation and handovers. If no one objects, I will treat this as the agreed core list for D1 and build T2 around it.
That list looks complete to me. It covers both safety and emotional needs. No objections from my side to using it as the base for the integrated routine.
Works for me as well. It is good that emotional check-ins and transitions are explicitly there, they often get forgotten when days are busy.
Agree with the list. Having documentation and handovers as a task will help us protect time for it.

Next, we need to agree which pain points we tackle first in the new routine (D2). From what you all shared, I see these as top candidates: a) clashes between hygiene tasks and meal/med times, b) inconsistent snack times causing distress, c) unclear timing and responsibility for cleaning shared spaces and toys, d) poor visibility on when children move between ward and childcare, e) weak handover notes on mood, appetite, and incidents. Are these the right top priorities for the first version, or is something else more urgent?

I agree with that list. For me the most urgent are the clashes between hygiene and meals/meds, and the unclear cleaning responsibilities. Those have direct safety implications. The movement between ward and childcare is also important but might be easier to improve once we have a shared timetable.

From my side, the biggest impact on children is inconsistent snack times and being pulled out of activities without warning. If the new routine can give us clearer windows for ward procedures and for childcare activities, that would already reduce a lot of upset.
I would keep handover notes in the priority list too. When mood and appetite are not passed on, we sometimes miss early signs that a child is not coping well.
For me the hardest part is when meals arrive while we are still washing or changing beds. If we can fix that, the rest will already feel more manageable.

Based on your replies, I suggest we lock in these as the top pain points to address in the first version of the integrated routine: 1) avoid clashes between hygiene tasks and meals/meds, 2) stabilise snack times and avoid conflicts with procedures and activities, 3) clarify timing and responsibility for cleaning shared spaces, toys, and equipment, 4) improve visibility and predictability of movements between ward and childcare, 5) strengthen handover notes on mood, appetite, and incidents. I will mark this as our agreed focus for D2 unless anyone disagrees today.
Happy with that focus list. It matches what we struggle with most on the ward.
Agreed from childcare side as well. Those five points will already make a big difference for children and families.

threads.thread_goal: Review and finalise the draft integrated routine and hygiene checklist.

messages.text: I have uploaded a first draft of the integrated routine and meal schedule as A3, based on A1 and our agreed core tasks and pain points (T2, T5). It is structured in morning, midday, afternoon, and evening blocks for both ward and childcare, with shared cleaning slots. I also sketched a hygiene checklist draft for A2 to cover rooms, toys, and shared equipment (T3). Can you review and flag anything that will not work in practice before we take it to nursing and infection control?

Thanks for pulling this together. Looking at A3, I like that morning hygiene is clearly before breakfast trays and meds, and that there is a fixed toy cleaning slot after the morning activity. One concern: the afternoon snack is at 15:30 for all ages. For younger children in childcare, that might be a bit late if lunch is at 12:00. Could we allow a slightly earlier snack window for them without clashing with ward procedures?

On the childcare side of A3, the 10:00–11:00 activity block and the 14:00–15:00 movement block look good. It helps that there are protected windows where ward procedures are less likely. For A2, I like that toys are grouped by type. Could we add a quick visual reminder for which toys must be disinfected after each use versus once per day? That would help when we are juggling several children.

From the ward perspective, the shared cleaning slots in A3 at 11:00 and 17:00 are helpful. I am a bit unsure about the time you set for evening wash, 19:00–19:30. On some days, visitors stay until 19:30. Maybe we need a flexible window like 18:30–20:00 with a note to coordinate with families.

I like that the routine shows when we should clean toys and meal areas. On A2, I am not sure how often we are supposed to clean door handles and bed rails. It says several times per day but does not say exactly when. Maybe we can tie it to the main blocks so it is easier to remember.

Good catch on the snack time. We can adjust A3 so that childcare has a 14:30–15:00 snack window, while the ward keeps 15:30–16:00 to avoid clashing with afternoon meds. I will mark that in T5 and check with dietary services about tray timing. On evening wash, I agree with making it a window 18:30–20:00 with a note to coordinate with families and nursing.

On A2, I can add a column that clearly says: after each use, once per shift, once per day. For example, mouth toys and sensory items for younger children would be after each use, board games once per day, and large equipment like mats once per shift. I will also tie door handles and bed rails to the start of each main block (morning, midday, afternoon, evening) so it is easier to remember, as suggested.

I like the idea of linking high-touch surfaces to the main time blocks. Maybe we can phrase it in A2 as: before breakfast, before lunch, before afternoon snack, and after evening wash. That way it lines up with A3 and is easy to brief at shift start.

One more thought: in A3, the handover and documentation slots are at 07:00–07:15 and 19:45–20:00. On busy days that might be tight. Could we extend them slightly or at least add a note that if tasks run over, we prioritise mood, appetite, and incidents in the notes?

Given the staffing constraint, I am hesitant to extend the time blocks too much, but we can add a clear note in A3 and A2 that if time is short, we always record mood, appetite, and any incidents first. We can also remind everyone that the handover template we will use later will prompt those fields.
That wording works for me. It is easy to explain to new staff: clean before each main meal or snack and after evening wash.
The extra column on A2 will help a lot. Sometimes I am not sure if I should clean a toy right away or wait until the end of the shift.

To move us towards sign-off on the routine blocks (D3): with the changes discussed (earlier childcare snack window, flexible evening wash window, clarified handover focus), is anyone still seeing a major clash between care, cleaning, meals, and activities in A3? If not, I suggest we treat this version as ready to review with one nurse and the childcare coordinator as required in T2 and T5.
From my side, the updated A3 looks workable and respects medication and treatment patterns as far as we can plan them. I am comfortable taking this version to the head nurse for a quick check.
No major clashes from childcare side either. The protected activity windows and snack timing look good. Happy to have our childcare coordinator review it as the next step.
I am fine with the time blocks as they are now. The notes about handover priorities help with the time pressure.

On the hygiene checklist (A2), to close D4 we need to be clear on responsibilities. I propose: ward assistants handle rooms, bed rails, and shared ward equipment; childcare staff handle toys and childcare room surfaces; both share responsibility for corridor play areas depending on where the child is at the time. I will send this version to infection control for feedback as part of T3. Any concerns with that split?
That split makes sense to me. Maybe just add a note that if a child uses ward equipment in the childcare room, the person who used it last is responsible for cleaning it before it goes back.
Agree with the split and with the extra note. It matches how we usually work, just more explicit.
I am ok with that. It helps to know clearly who should clean what.

Great, I will update A2 with that responsibility split and the extra note about shared equipment, then send it to infection control. Once they confirm, we can treat this as the final checklist for the pilot, covering D4.

threads.thread_goal: Align on the activity plan and how to support children emotionally during the new routine.

messages.text: I have drafted a weekly activity plan as A4 to fit into the time blocks in A3 (T4). It includes two structured activities per day: one in the morning (craft, story circle, sensory play) and one in the afternoon (movement, music, small group games). There are also suggestions for quick comfort activities we can use on the ward when children cannot come to childcare. Can you look at A4 and share if the activities feel realistic for mixed ages and different medical conditions?

Looking at A4, I like that each day has a calmer option and a more active one. For children on the ward who are attached to equipment, the sensory and story-based activities will work well. For the movement sessions, we might need a seated version for those who cannot stand or walk. Maybe we can add a short note for each activity on how to adapt it for limited mobility or high fatigue.

I like the weekly rhythm in A4: Monday more settling, midweek more active, Friday lighter. For emotional support, could we build in a short check-in question at the start of each group activity, like choosing a colour or face card to show how they feel? That might help us pick up who needs extra one-to-one time later in the day.

From the ward side, the quick comfort activities list is very useful. Things like short story cards, breathing games, and simple drawing are realistic at the bedside. Could we also add a couple of ideas for supporting siblings who visit, so they do not feel left out?
I like the plan but I am not sure how to handle days when a child is very tired or in pain. Should we still try to involve them in the group activity or just offer the comfort options?

Good point on adaptations. I can add a second line under each activity in A4 with ideas like: seated version, shorter duration, or using smaller movements. For example, for movement games we can use hand and arm actions or balloon play at the bedside.

I like the check-in idea. We can standardise it so that at the start of each structured activity we ask children to pick a colour or picture that matches their mood. I will add that to A4 and also suggest that we note any strong reactions in the handover template later.

On days when a child is very tired or in pain, I would lean towards offering the comfort options and a shorter, quieter version of the activity, maybe at the bedside. We should not push them into group sessions if it increases distress. Maybe A4 can say that participation is encouraged but optional, and comfort activities are always available.

I will add a small section in A4 for siblings: simple joint drawing, shared story time, or helping choose music. That way they can be included without taking focus away from the child who is admitted.

To prepare for D5, we should decide which activities are mandatory during the pilot and which are optional. My suggestion: mandatory: one structured group activity per day in childcare (morning or afternoon depending on the day), daily emotional check-in at the start of that activity, and at least one comfort activity offered to each child on the ward. Optional: the second structured activity of the day and any extra themed sessions. What do you think?

I support that split. Making one structured activity and the emotional check-in mandatory keeps things realistic with our staffing, and the comfort activity on the ward is important for children who cannot join groups.
Agree. On the ward, having at least one comfort activity per child per day as a target feels achievable, especially if we can use short options like story cards or drawing.
That sounds doable. It helps to know what is expected every day and what we can add if we have more time.

I am happy with that proposal. I will mark in A4 which activities are mandatory during the pilot and which are optional add-ons. That way when we collect feedback later for T9, we can see how often the optional ones were used.

Great, then for D5 we will define as mandatory during the pilot: 1) one structured group activity per day in childcare, 2) emotional check-in at the start of that activity, 3) at least one comfort activity per child per day on the ward. All other activities in A4 will be optional. I will note this so we can explain it clearly to staff before the pilot.

threads.thread_goal: Prepare for the pilot week, including handover process and logging of incidents.

messages.text: We are aiming to start the one-week pilot of the integrated routine next Monday (T8). I have drafted a handover notes template as A6 for T7 and linked it to the time blocks in A3. A7 will be used to log any deviations and incidents during the pilot. In this thread we need to agree how and when to use A6 each shift (D6) and what we count as an incident that must go into A7 (D7).

Looking at A6, the sections are hygiene, meals, mood, and incidents, plus a free notes area. For D6, I suggest we use A6 at the end of each shift, but start filling it during the shift so it is not all left to the last 10 minutes. Maybe we can agree that we update it briefly after each main block in A3 and then do a quick review at handover.

I like the idea of updating A6 during the shift. Maybe we can say: short entries after breakfast, lunch, and dinner blocks, and then a final check at handover. That way we do not forget mood changes or missed meals.
I am a bit worried about having time to fill A6 during busy mornings. Could we agree on the minimum we must write if we are short on time?

From childcare side, using A6 at the end of the morning and end of the afternoon would work well. That lines up with our activity blocks in A3. For incidents, I think we should definitely log any time a child becomes very distressed during transitions or activities, not just physical issues.

If time is tight, I suggest we always prioritise three things in A6: 1) any missed or refused meals, 2) notable mood changes (very withdrawn, very agitated), and 3) any incidents. We can add that guidance at the top of A6 so it is clear.

To make D6 concrete, how about this: each shift uses one A6 sheet per child; we add quick notes after breakfast, lunch, and dinner blocks, plus after the main activity in childcare; then we do a 5-minute review at handover where outgoing staff highlight any red flags. That keeps it structured without adding a separate long meeting.
That sounds workable. The 5-minute review at handover is important so the incoming team knows what to focus on.
I can work with that, especially with the guidance on what to prioritise when we are busy.
Agreed. For childcare we can align the notes with the end of the morning and afternoon activity blocks.

Ok, then for D6 we will state: A6 is used for each child, updated briefly after breakfast, lunch, dinner, and the main activity block, with a 5-minute review at each shift handover. If time is short, we prioritise meals, mood, and incidents. I will update A6 accordingly.

Next we need to be clear on what counts as an incident for A7 during the pilot (D7). I propose we include: 1) any fall or physical injury, 2) any medication or meal timing issue linked to the new routine, 3) any hygiene lapse (missed cleaning slot, shared toy not cleaned as per A2), 4) any episode of severe distress linked to routine changes or transitions, 5) any situation where the routine had to be significantly changed for safety reasons. Does that feel like the right scope?

I would add any near-miss where we caught a problem just in time, for example almost giving a meal too close to a procedure because of a timing confusion. Those are useful to learn from even if nothing bad happened.

From childcare side, I would also log if a child refuses to attend activities for several days because of anxiety about the new routine. That might show us that we need to adjust how we explain changes.
Agree with the list and the additions. It might help to have a simple tick-box in A7 for each type of incident so we do not spend too long writing.
I am ok with that list. It is clear what we should log.

Thanks all. To close D7, we will define incidents for A7 as: falls or injuries, medication or meal timing issues linked to the routine, hygiene lapses against A2, severe distress linked to routine or transitions, significant changes to the routine for safety, near-misses where a problem was caught in time, and repeated refusal to join activities due to anxiety about the new routine. I will add simple tick-box categories for these in A7.

For T8, I will prepare a short one-page summary for staff explaining: the key time blocks from A3, how to use A6 during shifts, and what to log in A7. I will also ask the head nurse to confirm we can start the pilot on Monday and that they are comfortable with the logging approach.

threads.thread_goal: Review pilot results and decide on adjustments before wider rollout.

messages.text: We have completed the five weekday pilot of the integrated routine (T8). I have summarised the main observations and incidents in A7 and updated A3, A2, and A4 with comments. Overall, the routine was followed on most shifts, with a few deviations around late procedures and unexpected admissions. In this thread we need to decide which changes from the pilot we keep, modify, or drop for the final routine (D8) and what to include in the orientation guide A5 (T10, T6).

From my shifts, the biggest win was moving morning hygiene clearly before breakfast and meds. A7 shows fewer clashes and fewer cold meals. I think we should definitely keep that. One issue was the fixed afternoon snack time on the ward; on two days, procedures ran late and we had to improvise. Maybe we need a small buffer window in A3 rather than a single fixed time.

On the childcare side, A7 shows that the emotional check-ins at the start of activities worked well. Children liked choosing colours or faces, and it helped us spot who needed extra support. I strongly suggest we keep that. We had a couple of incidents where children were called back to the ward mid-activity, but less often than before. The shared timetable in A3 seems to have helped.

Using A6 for handovers made a clear difference. A7 shows fewer missed notes about appetite and mood. I think we should keep the structure but maybe simplify the free text area; some staff found it hard to know what to write there.

For me, the checklist A2 helped remember toy cleaning, but I still missed a couple of door handle cleanings on very busy mornings. Maybe we can add a small visual reminder near the sinks or on the trolley.

Agree that morning hygiene before breakfast and meds should stay as is. On the afternoon snack, A7 shows three deviations where we had to move it later due to procedures. We could adjust A3 to show a snack window, for example 15:00–16:00, with a note to coordinate with nursing. That would reflect what we actually did during the pilot.

Visual reminders are a good idea. Maybe we can add a one-page summary from A2 with icons for high-touch surfaces and place it in the ward and childcare rooms. That could also go into A5 so new staff see it on day one.

On feedback from children and families (T9), several parents said they liked knowing roughly when activities and meals would happen, and that their children seemed calmer with the more predictable routine. A few asked for more flexibility on days when their child had a lot of tests. So I think we should keep the structure but emphasise in A5 that the routine can be adapted around medical needs.

Yes, in the informal feedback I collected for T9, children mentioned they liked knowing when snack and play would happen, and they especially liked the music and craft days in A4. One child said they felt rushed on a day with many tests, so we might want to add a note that on heavy treatment days, comfort activities can replace group sessions.
For A6, maybe we can replace the big free text box with two short prompts: what went well and what to watch out for next shift. That might make it easier to fill and still capture key points.
I like the idea of icons. It would help me remember even when I am in a hurry.
Good suggestion. I will adjust A6 to have two short prompts instead of a large free text area. That should also make it easier to explain in A5.

To move towards D8, it might help to group changes into keep, modify, and drop. From what we have so far: Keep: morning hygiene before breakfast and meds, emotional check-ins, use of A6 at each handover, comfort activities as part of A4. Modify: afternoon snack as a window, A6 free text area into two prompts, add visual reminders from A2, clarify flexibility around heavy treatment days in A3 and A5. Drop: I am not sure we have anything to fully drop, maybe just some of the optional activities that were never used.

I agree with that grouping. For the optional activities in A4 that we did not use, I suggest we keep them in a separate ideas list rather than in the main weekly plan. That way new staff are not overwhelmed when they read A5.
I am comfortable with keeping and modifying as you described. I do not see anything that needs to be completely removed, just clarified.
Same here. The changes you listed match what I experienced on my shifts.

Based on the pilot data in A7 and your comments, I will update A3 to show the snack window and flexibility notes, A2 to include icons and clearer high-touch reminders, A4 to mark optional activities separately, A6 to use the two prompts, and A5 to explain the routine, emotional check-ins, and how to adapt on heavy treatment days. Once these updates are done, we can present the final package to the ward manager and childcare coordinator as part of T10.

Then for D8, we can say: we will keep the main structure of the integrated routine and hygiene checklist from the pilot, modify snack timing to a window, simplify and strengthen A6, add visual hygiene reminders from A2, and move unused optional activities in A4 to an ideas list. Nothing is fully dropped, but some elements are moved out of the core routine. This will form the basis of the final routine and orientation guide A5.
That summary matches my understanding. It will be helpful for explaining to families that we tested the routine and adjusted it based on what we saw and heard.
